conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how mothers are feeling in the weeks after birth, because emotional ups and downs are so common and deserve attention.

We’ll use a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten questions about your mood, anxiety, and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our team. We want you to feel safe and supported while we complete this together.

When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. We’ll start with the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe when your baby did something amusing or during everyday moments? How often would you say that happened?

Oh, yeah—my little guy made this goofy face yesterday while he was feeding and milk dribbled everywhere. My partner and I both burst out laughing. I’d say most days I still find things funny… maybe not quite as easily as before I was pregnant, but I can still laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, definitely—I still laugh most days. Like I said, the baby did something silly yesterday and I couldn’t help but giggle.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like taking him out in the stroller when the weather’s nice or having coffee with a friend who’s dropping by tomorrow. It’s not every single moment, but I still get that little spark of “can’t wait” pretty often.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If he spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think, “Maybe I ate something that bothered him,” but I don’t beat myself up. I figure we’re both learning and tomorrow’s a new day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes, yeah—like I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds different, even though he’s fine. It’s not constant, just little flashes of worry that pop up out of nowhere and then fade.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like panic. I get those quick worries about the baby, but it never turns into a real scared or panicky feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, when he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel a bit swamped. It passes once he finally sleeps or I get a shower, though. Most of the time I feel like I’m keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping okay—well, as okay as you can with a newborn. Once I settle him, I can get back to sleep pretty easily. I’m not lying there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say sad or miserable—more like tired and a bit overwhelmed sometimes, but it lifts when I see the baby smile or when my partner brings me coffee.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up once this week when I accidentally bumped the crib and startled him, but it was just a moment and I was fine after I cuddled him.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that most days you still laugh easily when your baby does something funny and you look forward to small outings like stroller walks or coffee with a friend. Occasional <sym>worry</sym> flashes about the baby's breathing pop up, yet they fade quickly and you do not feel <sym>panicky</sym>. When chores pile up you can feel momentarily swamped, but a shower or the baby's smile lifts your mood. You denied persistent <sym>sadness</sym>, trouble sleeping beyond newborn wake-ups, and any thoughts of self-harm, noting you are generally keeping your head above water.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes occasional unexpected worries about baby's breathing that appear and fade, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to 0-3 per item; your total was 5, well below the 8-point threshold for possible <med>postpartum depression</med>. You retain the ability to laugh and anticipate pleasant events (Q1, Q2 = 0) and lack the pervasive low mood, guilt, sleep disruption from <sym>unhappiness</sym>, or <sym>tearfulness</sym> seen in <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Brief situational worries and mild overwhelm are common postpartum adjustments rather than clinical <med>anxiety</med> or <med>depression</med>. No safety concerns were endorsed on Q10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum follow-up with your midwife or obstetrician
2. Re-screen with EPDS at 6-week visit or sooner if mood worsens
3. Practice self-compassion: accept help with chores, rest when baby sleeps
4. Maintain social contacts like the friend coffee date you look forward to
5. Seek support promptly if worries intensify or mood drops
6. Call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report, clinician review  
Gravida/parity: G1P1, 3 wk post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild, episodic “flashes” of unexplained worry about infant health (Q4)  
- Occasional feeling of being “swamped” when daily tasks accumulate, quickly resolves with support or infant sleep (Q6)

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic attacks, sleep-onset or maintenance insomnia linked to mood, tearfulness beyond brief situational episode, self-harm ideation (Q1–3, 5, 7–10)

Observed pattern  
- Maintains capacity for pleasure, laughter, and future-oriented enjoyment  
- Absence of cognitive or somatic depressive symptoms; no safety concerns  
- Transient anxiety appears situationally and self-limited

Screening impression  
Current responses do not indicate elevated probability for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder; no additional risk flags identified at this time. Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
